newsitem.title: INDIA: India banks turn corner in 96/97, worries linger.
newsitem.headline: India banks turn corner in 96/97, worries linger.

text.p: India's state-run banks swung back into profit in 1996/97 (April-March) but falling interest rates will lower revenue streams and increased credit offtake could see a spurt in non-performing assets, analysts said Wednesday.

Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor Chakravarty Rangarajan said on Monday state-run banks were poised to post a combined net profit of around 30 billion rupees for 1996/97 (April-March) against a net loss of 3.71 billion the previous year.

But the bulk of these profits will come from a handful of banks with just four out of 27 state-run banks contributing more than two-thirds of the projected total. Results from most banks are still to be posted.
The State Bank of India reported a 1996/97 net of 13.29 billion rupees, Bank of India 3.6 billion, Bank of Baroda 2.76 billion and Oriental Bank of Commerce 1.8 billion.
The drop in interest rates has a double-edged effect, and in the past year the impact has benefitted banks' balance sheets.
"An improvement in profits will be mainly because provisions on account of revaluation of investments will be less this year," said S.R. Krishnan, banking analyst at Peregrine Capital India Ltd.
He said lower interest rates this year will lead to lower provisions, for the 50 percent investments banks are reuired to mark to markets -- value at market prices.
If the market price prevailing on the date of valuation is lower than the cost of acquisition, the bank has to provide for the difference.
In a falling interest rate scenario, security prices rise and there is less pressure on banks to provide for depreciation on investments marked to market.
But the poor quality of the loan portfolios of state-run banks remains a major concern, analysts said.

Half-way through fiscal 1996/97, RBI governor Rangarajan said non-performing assets constituted around 19 percent of bank advances but hoped for a reduction to around 10 percent in the next two years.
"The fact is that most of the state-run banks have a high percentage of non-performing assets (NPAs)," said an analyst at a U.S. investment bank, who did not want to be identified.

"The poor loan growth last year helped banks to consolidate and clean up their loan books," he said. "But if the lower interest rates trigger off a growth in loan disbursals this year, we will see NPAs go up."
Further, falling interest rates will also hit revenue streams, the analyst warned.
"Banks will benefit from the provisions (on investments) angle but revenue streams will suffer.
"In a falling interest rate regime, banks are hit as the lower rates are straightaway applicable to all loans.
"But in the case of deposits, the revised rates take effect only on fresh deposits and banks remain locked into their older deposits at the higher rates," he said.
Bank performance in 1996/97 had also been helped higher interest rates in the first half of last year.
"Interest rates started dropping only in the second half of the year," the analyst said.
State Bank of India, the largest commercial bank, last Saturday cuts its prime lending rate to 13.5 percent from 14.0 percent, and in March 1996 it was 16.5 percent.
